title: AAdvantage® Cash App.
subtitle: Flight attendants earn bonuses for the AAdvantage® Cash card applications they bring in, but could only check on them through a web portal. We designed a mobile app that puts their application status and earnings first.

glance.Problem: Flight attendants could only check the status of their card applications on a web portal, which didn't fit a job that's always on the move.
glance.Contribution: UX and visual design: MVP scope, wireframes, testing, typography, components, prototypes, and the Bonus Booster.
glance.Outcome: A mobile app that leads with application status and projected earnings.

sections.label: Problem
sections.heading: Status checks lived on a web portal.
paras: Flight attendants in the AAdvantage® Cash program earn bonuses and trips for the credit card applications they submit, but the only way to check their status was a web portal. That doesn't fit a job where they're always on the move. On top of that, another company had already built a UI mockup before our team came in, and it was made with very little research. The visuals lacked depth and the layouts had almost no white space.

sections.label: Context
sections.heading: Starting from someone else's mockup.
paras: This was a 2021–2022 project where I owned UX and visual design. Because the team inherited someone else's mockup, it didn't start like a normal UX project. After a lot of back and forth about which features mattered, I suggested focusing on an MVP that would help users and still satisfy stakeholders. The team ran a design sprint, built personas from research on flight attendants, then moved through several rounds of wireframes and two rounds of unguided user testing.

sections.label: Research
sections.heading: What flight attendants told us.
bullets: Most flight attendants wanted the information to be straightforward.
Their biggest concern was seeing the status of the applications they'd submitted.
In the first round of testing, they called out the lack of color in the app.
When the final version was presented, they liked the updated visuals and the Bonus Booster.

sections.label: Solution
sections.heading: Status and earnings first.
paras: The team rebuilt the homepage around current application status (received vs. approved) and projected earnings, so the thing flight attendants cared about most was the first thing they saw. I also designed the Bonus Booster, a slider that shows what they could earn at each bonus tier (Base, Tier 1, Tier 2). I handled typography, components, sizing, and prototypes, while teammates created onboarding artwork and refined the visuals.

sections.label: Next steps
sections.heading: What I'd have tracked.
paras: The app launched shortly after I moved on from the project. I didn't get to see the post-launch results, but the last round of testing was a good sign: flight attendants responded well to the updated visuals and the Bonus Booster, which were the two areas the first round had flagged.
If I'd stayed on, I would have tracked:
bullets: Adoption: how many flight attendants switched from the web portal to the app.
Bonus Booster impact: whether seeing the next bonus tier led them to submit more applications.
Support requests: whether fewer flight attendants had to ask about their application status.
after: I'd also want to test with veteran flight attendants. They're the most resistant to change, and the most likely to stop using the app.
